This tutorial introduces to data augmentation with the package `housepi`. We'll walk through the process of associating augmented variable to individuals to then proceed with standard model generation and inference. We start by loading the package:

```{r}
library(housepi)
```

## Estimate incubation periods distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a database which is not a household survey. Instead we consider a simulated report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.

```{r}
delays <- read.csv("data/delays.csv")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(head(read.csv("data/delays.csv")))
```

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate the respective parameters augmenting the exposure and onset times, modeled as uniformly distributed in the reported ranges. To take into account right censoring, we modify the maximum values to allow times to be within the day

```{r}
delays[["exposure_max"]] <- delays[["exposure_max"]] + 1 - 1e-5
delays[["onset_max"]] <- delays[["onset_max"]] + 1 - 1e-5
```

We generate the model as showed in the [walkthrough](walkthrough.html):

```{r}
# generate the model
hemi1 <- generate_model("example_augm_delay_incubation")

# parameter definitions
params <- ParameterFrame$new(list(
  shape = list(x = 1, 
               prior = "uniform", args = list(min = 0, max = 5),
               rule = "lognorm", rule_args = list(sdlog = 1)),
  scale = list(x = 1,
               prior = "uniform", args = list(min = 0, max = 5),
               rule = "lognorm", rule_args = list(sdlog = 1))
  ))$df

# general setup
setup <- list(num_iter = 30000, num_adapt = 2500, burn_in = 2000,
              thinning = 25, seed = 576125013)

# associate data, parameters and setup
build_model(hemi1, data = delays, params = params, setup = setup)
```

The code considers the database as a community of individuals living in households of size 1.

### Build Augmented Variables

Similarly to parameter definitions, for augmented variables we provide a DataFrame or a file with the models and proposer rules needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo. However, augmented variable definitions are more delicate, since they can depend on data or parameters. We state which value should be imported from data formatting it as a string "<value-name>`@D`". Here we associate to each individual an exposure and an onset time.

```{r}
augm <- AugmentedFrame(list(
  # define 'exposure' time
  exposure = list(
    x = "exposure_min@D", # start from exposure_min (data)
    model = "uniform",    # associate a uniform model
    args = list(min = "exposure_min@D",  # 'exposure_min' (data)
                max = "exposure_max@D"), # 'exposure_max' (data)
    rule = "normal",      # rule for Metropolis move is normal
    rule_args = list(sd = 0.125)         # std. dev. of normal rule
  ),
  
  # define 'onset' time
  onset = list(
    x = "onset_max@D",    # start from onset_max (data)
    model = "uniform",    # ...
    args = list(min = "onset_min@D", max = "onset_max@D"),
    rule = "normal",
    rule_args = list(sd = "rule_sd@P")   # 'rule_sd' (parameters)
  )
))$df

# associate augmented variable definitions
build_model(hemi1, augm = augm)
```

We run the inference and we extract the results

```{r}
mcmc_trace <- run_inference(hemi1)
coda::traceplot(mcmc_trace)
results <- summary(mcmc_trace)
```

## Augment onset times

We use the default model "augm_onset_single_intr", where surveys are conditioned on single introduction and follow the times of onset.

```{r}
hemi2 <- generate_model("augm_onset_single_intr")

setup <- list(num_iter = 30000, num_adapt = 2500, burn_in = 2000,
              thinning = 25, seed = 576125013)

build_model(hemi2, data = "data/survey.csv", 
            params = "data/params.csv", setup = setup)

# store the choice of the parameters to be used in the simulation
params <- hemi2$params()
```

This time we have loaded the parameter definitions directly from a file

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(head(read.csv("data/params.csv")))
```

We propose the following augmented variable definitions

```{r}
augm <- AugmentedFrame$new()

augm$add(name = "onset_date", x = 1,
         rule = "normal", rule_args = list(sd = 0.25),
         range = list(min = -7), init_rand = FALSE)

augm$add(name = "incub_period", model = "gamma",
         args = list(shape = "inc_shape@P", scale = "inc_scale@P"),
         rule = "model", range = list(max = "inc_max@P"))

build_model(hemi2, augm = augm$df)
```

## Simulate an Augmented Model

We run a simulation with the method `simulate`.

```{r}
# override status of the dataset according to simulation 
hemi2$simulate()

# load the simulated dataset
df <- hemi$data()
# show the results of the simulation 
head(df[c("status", "incub_period", "onset_date")])
```

We can see that in addition to the status, the simulation also associates the values of the augmented variables: the incubation period and the onset time.

As a sanity check, we can verify that inference returns the parameters used for the simulation.

```{r}
mcmc_trace <- run_inference(hemi2)
coda::traceplot(mcmc_trace)
results <- summary(mcmc_trace)

# collect the information for the check
inames <- params[params["infer"] == TRUE, "name"]
data.frame(Expec = params[params["infer"] == TRUE, "value"],
           Mean = results[["statistics"]][inames, "Mean"],
           Q2.5 = results[["quantiles"]][inames, "2.5%"],
           Q97.5 = results[["quantiles"]][inames, "97.5%"])
```

Remember that templated models do simulate the sampling process.
